Hospital planners need to understand not only how long patients typically stay, but how those stays add up across admissions to create pressure on bed capacity. A small increase in typical length of stay can translate into a large number of additional bed-days when multiplied across many admissions. The “extra typical bed-days” measure compares each year with the 2014 baseline: it multiplies the change in median length of stay by the number of eligible stroke or heart attack admissions in that year. It includes eligible admissions ending in hospital death and counts a same-day stay as one day. Because it uses the median rather than the mean, rare very long stays do not dominate the estimate. It is a practical planning indicator, not a direct measure of actual occupied beds.
